name: Argo CD
lede: The GitOps controller we already run. The work is making it converge, not choosing it.
what: A CNCF Graduated controller that continuously reconciles clusters to what is declared in Git, with a UI, RBAC, multi-cluster targets and sync waves.
apart: Versus Flux: a first-class UI and ApplicationSets for fleets; Flux is lighter and more composable but has no UI. The 3.x line added a resources explorer and ApplicationSet views.
stand: Already ours. Turn on auto-sync with self-heal, and write the upgrade ticket to the current 3.x line. ⚠️ Confirm the exact version against the release notes.
src: ArgoCon and the Argo maintainer track, KubeCon NA 2026
note: The ArgoCon point we both took away: the controller isn't the gap, the manual sync button is.

name: ApplicationSets + progressive sync
lede: One definition fanned out to every cluster, in waves rather than all at once.
what: An Argo CD controller that generates Applications from generators (cluster list, label selector, Git directories, pull requests). Progressive sync rolls them out in ordered steps with health checks between.
apart: It selects clusters by label, the cheapest route to a constraint vocabulary. It is a templating controller, not a scheduler: no health input, no rescheduling when a cluster disappears.
stand: Trial progressive sync on one platform component across non-prod; use label selectors as the cluster interface from day one.
src: Argo CD docs; LinkedIn's canary pipeline talk, KubeCon NA 2026
note: Name the limit every time it comes up: placement that reacts to cluster health is Karmada or OCM territory, not this.

name: Argo CD source hydrator
lede: Commit the rendered YAML back to Git, so what's in Git is what runs.
what: Argo CD renders Helm or Kustomize and commits the output to a hydrated branch. Reviews read real manifests instead of a chart plus values someone renders in their head.
apart: Readable diffs are what make PR-based promotion work, and GitOps Promoter is designed around them. Kargo works mostly on dry manifests, so the hydrator matters more if we pick Promoter.
stand: Trial it as part of the Promoter spike, not as a separate project.
src: Argo CD 3.x release line; ArgoCon, KubeCon NA 2026
note: This is the quiet prerequisite for the promotion decision. Spike them together.

name: Argo Rollouts
lede: Traffic-weighted canaries and blue-green, with automated analysis and rollback.
what: Replaces a Deployment with a Rollout: setWeight and pause steps shift traffic, an AnalysisTemplate queries Prometheus, CloudWatch or a job, and a failed analysis rolls back automatically.
apart: Pluggable traffic routers: a mesh, an ingress, ALB, or the Gateway API plugin, which decouples canaries from a mesh decision. Versus Flagger: tighter Argo CD integration and UI.
stand: Pilot on one user-facing HTTP app. ⚠️ Sources disagree on whether the Gateway API plugin is alpha or stable; check the docs first.
src: Argo Rollouts docs; ArgoCon AWS cases, KubeCon NA 2026
note: For cluster-critical services with no traffic to split, the namespace-scoped canary is the better fit.

name: GitOps Promoter
lede: Our lean for promotion: every environment change is a pull request.
what: An Argo Labs project that promotes between environments by opening PRs against per-environment branches, gated by commit statuses that prove the checks passed.
apart: No state outside Git: the PR is the audit trail, readable by anyone with repo access. Designed around hydrated manifests. Linear pipelines today; DAG promotion is on its roadmap.
stand: Our preferred option going into the spike. Watch for: per-environment commit statuses wired by hand, and less adoption data than Kargo.
src: GitOps Promoter docs; ArgoCon's agent-ready checklist, KubeCon NA 2026
note: ArgoCon showed it as the traceability mechanism in the agent-ready checklist, which is part of why we lean this way: it serves the agent path too.

name: Kargo
lede: The serious alternative: a promotion control plane with its own UI.
what: An Akuity project modelling promotion as Warehouses (sources), Freight (versioned bundles) and Stages, with promotion steps and verification between them.
apart: Built for complex multi-stage pipelines and fleet-to-target mapping, with a UI release managers can live in. ⚠️ Its adoption figure in our notes is vendor-reported.
stand: Spike it second. It wins if what we want is a release-management UI across many targets rather than PRs as the record.
src: Akuity; ArgoCon fleet demo, KubeCon NA 2026
note: Akuity maintains both Argo CD and Kargo, so read their comparisons accordingly. That's why we want our own spike.

name: Stakater Reloader
lede: Restart what consumes a ConfigMap or Secret when it changes.
what: A small controller that watches ConfigMaps and Secrets and triggers a rolling restart of the Deployments, StatefulSets and DaemonSets that reference them.
apart: Annotation-driven and tiny, with no sidecar. The alternative is hash-annotation tricks in every chart, which teams forget.
stand: Adopt first. Without it a GitOps config change appears to succeed while pods keep serving the old value.
note: The cheapest item on the path, and it protects the 'Git is the state of the world' claim.

name: Kyverno
lede: Policy as Kubernetes YAML, for what in-tree CEL can't express.
what: A CNCF policy engine that validates, mutates, generates and cleans up resources, with policy reports and a CLI that runs the same policies in CI.
apart: Versus OPA Gatekeeper: policies in YAML rather than Rego, plus generation and mutation. It now authors CEL-based policies too, riding the in-tree direction instead of competing with it.
stand: Our policy layer: CI shift-left, change-window gating against a projected CRD, and reports.
src: Kyverno maintainer track; "Signed, Sealed, Denied" (AT&T), KubeCon NA 2026
note: The change-window CRD keeps the admission path from depending on the ITSM system being up.

name: Validating / MutatingAdmissionPolicy
lede: Admission policy built into the API server, written in CEL.
what: In-tree Kubernetes admission policies evaluated inside the API server with CEL expressions, bound to resources with policy bindings and parameters.
apart: No webhook: in-process evaluation, no TLS plumbing, nothing in the admission path that can be down. The trade-off is expressiveness: no external data lookups.
stand: The default for simple validations and mutations; Kyverno for the rest.
src: "Goodbye Webhooks, Hello CEL", Greg Bray, Google, KubeCon NA 2026
note: The trade-off slide in Greg's deck is worth showing anyone who asks why not Kyverno for everything.

name: Falco
lede: Runtime detection: what happened after admission said yes.
what: A CNCF Graduated runtime security tool that watches syscalls and Kubernetes audit events via eBPF and alerts on rules: a shell in a container, an unexpected Secret read, a ConfigMap edited outside Argo.
apart: Detection, not prevention. Versus Tetragon: Falco has the larger rule library; Tetragon can enforce in-kernel. Either covers the gap admission policy leaves.
stand: Trial on one cluster with one out-of-band-change rule first.
src: "After Admission: Kernel Enforcement for Agents Kyverno Let In", KubeCon NA 2026
note: The one rule worth writing first: alert on any write to a Secret or ConfigMap that didn't come from Argo CD's service account.

name: Gateway API
lede: The successor to Ingress, and the router a traffic-weighted canary needs.
what: The Kubernetes routing API (Gateways, HTTPRoutes, GRPCRoutes) with role separation between platform and app teams and many implementations, including Istio.
apart: Portable across implementations and expressive enough for canaries and header routing. Ingress NGINX is retired, so it's the destination, not an option.
stand: Adopt, with an owner and a date. It also unlocks the Argo Rollouts Gateway API plugin. On no path, but on a clock.
src: Ingress NGINX retirement; Gateway API maintainer track, KubeCon NA 2026
note: This migration pays twice: the ingress move we have to make anyway, and the router canaries need.

name: Istio
lede: The mesh direction we're already committed to.
what: A service mesh providing mTLS identity, traffic policy and telemetry, in sidecar or ambient mode, with multicluster east-west gateways.
apart: Locality-aware failover sheds load to the remote region on outlier detection. Coinbase, with 79 prod clusters, named ambient as their direction. Multicluster discovery is O(n²): fine at two clusters, a cap beyond.
stand: Committed. Open item: sidecar versus ambient, in ISTIO-VS-GATEWAY-API.md. Budget mesh telemetry cardinality as a cost line.
src: Coinbase, mesh-native mTLS; "Breaking the O(n²) Wall" (Microsoft), KubeCon NA 2026
note: Locality failover only fires if outlier detection is actually configured.
